title: Rain and dew prayers
hook: on Shemini Atzeret and Passover the seasonal prayer switches between rain and dew

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashamnu, the confession said in the plural. Your line was we, not I. What did you take your share of? Today, a prayer that changes with the weather. Day six hundred thirty-one.

Someone in London, where it rains half the year, and someone in Phoenix, where it hardly rains at all, open the same prayer book in October. And on the same day, both start praying for rain. Not for their own city. For a small strip of land on the eastern Mediterranean, where the rains come between autumn and spring, and where, in ancient times, whether they came decided whether people ate. Twice a year, the Amidah changes one line, to follow the seasons of a land many of them have never lived in.
screen: `LONDON AND PHOENIX, IN OCTOBER.` → `BOTH PRAY FOR RAIN.` → `THE SEASONS OF ONE LAND.`

segments.voice: In the second blessing of the Amidah, the one about God's power, there's a seasonal line. In winter: mashiv haruach umorid hageshem, who makes the wind blow and the rain fall. Geshem means rain. The switch happens at Musaf on Shemini Atzeret, the day after Sukkot, just as the rainy season in the Land of Israel begins. The cantor, often dressed in white as on the High Holy Days, chants a special prayer for rain, Tefillat Geshem. Its medieval poem remembers the ancestors and water. Abraham, who followed God like flowing water. Isaac, whose servants dug wells. Jacob, who rolled the stone from the well. Moses, drawn from the water. And the tribes, who crossed the sea. Then, on the first day of Passover, as the rains end, the cantor chants a prayer for dew, Tefillat Tal. After that, many communities, especially in Israel and among Sephardim, say morid hatal, who makes the dew fall, all summer. Others say nothing until autumn. Why is rain in a blessing about God's power? The Talmud says there are three keys God keeps and gives to no messenger: the key of rain, the key of birth, and the key of bringing the dead to life. Rain sits in the same blessing as the hope of life restored. Dry seed, buried, comes up green. And dew? The rabbis taught that dew is never held back. It comes quietly, every summer night, even when nothing else falls. Rain is a request. Dew is a gift that's always there.
screen: `GESHEM: RAIN.` · `ANCESTORS AND WATER.` · `ON PASSOVER, THE PRAYER FOR DEW.` · `THE KEY OF RAIN.` · then, large: `RAIN AND DEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the season's weather. Settle, and breathe. Look outside, or picture the sky over you today. Is it wet or dry, warm or cold? Then picture the soil under the nearest tree, and what the season is doing to it. If you pray, this is a moment to give thanks for rain, or for dew, whichever the season brings. If not, simply thank the weather for keeping things alive. The bell holds the time.
Geshem. Rain. The prayer chanted on Shemini Atzeret, when the Amidah begins to praise the one who makes the rain fall.
Your line: rain and dew. Today, notice one thing that keeps you alive quietly, like dew, and one thing you have to ask for, like rain. Day six hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Tefillat Geshem is chanted in Musaf on Shemini Atzeret, after which 'who makes the wind blow and the rain fall' is added to the Amidah until Passover; Tefillat Tal is chanted on the first day of Passover, after which many communities say 'who makes the dew fall' through the summer.

original.note: Hebrew: rain, as in morid hageshem, who makes the rain fall.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer about the weather.
what it means: a yearly turn that ties prayer to the rains of one land, and to the hope of life returning.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Taanit 1:1–2 sets the dates; Taanit 2a's three keys put rain beside the revival of the dead.

notes: Taanit 2a: Rabbi Yochanan's three keys (rain, childbirth, resurrection); confirm.

Tefillat Geshem poem (Kalir) stanzas paraphrased: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, the twelve tribes; Aaron omitted for length. Abraham's line changed from 'stood by the waters' to 'followed God like flowing water' (zechor av nimshach acharecha kamayim); confirm the other stanza summaries.
'Dew is never held back' now attributed to the rabbis (Taanit 3a); confirm citation.
Morid hatal in summer: Sephardi and Israeli Ashkenazi practice; diaspora Ashkenazim generally omit; confirm.
The separate request for rain in the ninth blessing (v'ten tal umatar), starting in early December outside Israel, is not discussed.
